reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of AI use in government comes from the U.S. GAO's audit of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. Reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases.

The same GAO audit shows the management side lagging the deployment side. GAO found incomplete and inaccurate data in agency inventories, with five agencies providing comprehensive information for each reported use case while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories omitted required elements such as the AI life cycle stage, and two inventories included AI uses that agencies later determined were not AI. On compliance, ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and the Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. GAO also noted there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.

The most visible recent federal deployment is America.gov, launched September 29, 2026 by the General Services Administration and the National Design Studio under an executive order, per the White House fact sheet. It is described as a single digital point of entry where an individual can sign in, communicate in plain language, receive accurate answers, and, where authorized and technically available, complete government transactions. The fact sheet states that Americans can currently ask any question and get an up-to-date answer, and that later in the year they will be able to complete tasks like passport renewal and Medicare enrollment. Covered services are public-facing federal services serving more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period that can be accessed or applied for online, with tax filing services provided by the Internal Revenue Service and national-security-sensitive services provided by the Department of War and the Intelligence Community excluded. This site's own tracking adds that America.gov runs on Google Gemini and xAI Grok, that Phase 2 is planned for 2027 with Login.gov to handle applications and renewals, and that it offers no public API and its terms bar automated agents.

On the regulatory side, this site's AI laws tracker records 6,045 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database. Of the measures passed, 113 measures across 28 states were reviewed on September 18, 2026, and no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149; every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where the stakes are personal, the recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act.

The international and policy-monitoring sources in this set are thinner on measured adoption. Stanford HAI describes the AI Index as an independent initiative providing globally sourced data for policymakers, and states that this year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind. The OECD AI Policy Observatory describes its role as helping countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog about AI policy, with organizations developing advanced AI systems able to participate by submitting a report to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. Oxford Insights describes its work helping governments increase the impact of their public services through empowering teams and harnessing technology. None of these three pages reports a government adoption rate or an ROI figure.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical conclusions. The federal record shows that most planned government AI use cases are not yet in production, that inventories of what is running are often incomplete, and that acquisition guidance and workforce categories are still missing, so internal record-keeping and clear ownership matter as much as the model itself. The state legislative record shows that the question in each state is never whether you use AI but what you use it for, that a qualified person must stay in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, that people should be told when they are dealing with AI, and that the attorney general is the enforcer most deployers are likely to meet. The sources here report no ROI evidence for government AI, so any claim about returns would go beyond what this material shows.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index at Stanford HAI describes its mission as supplying unbiased, globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public, tracking and visualising data on the field. This year's edition, the page says, shows a widening gap between what AI can do and our readiness to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while governance and evaluation frameworks lag. The page states that previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It describes the programme as an independent Stanford HAI initiative led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, and notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez on regulatory frameworks.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports that 6,045 artificial intelligence bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It states that 113 enrolled measures across 28 states were compared as of September 18, 2026, and that no two states wrote the same law, though recurring choices appear. According to the page, only Colorado (CO SB189) and Texas (TX HB149) passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while other measures name single settings such as chatbots, political ads, insurance prior authorization, classrooms or state agencies. It says no state in the set created a new agency to enforce AI law, with attorneys general enforcing the larger laws and several states treating violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under consumer protection acts.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
